stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28-year-old primigravida at 34+2 weeks referred by her midwife for elevated blood pressure of 168/108 mmHg on two readings 15 minutes apart. She reports a frontal headache since morning and one episode of epigastric discomfort. There is no visual disturbance, no vaginal bleeding, and normal fetal movements. She has no prior hypertension, no chronic kidney disease, and no significant family history. Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein and she has bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin. Fetal heart rate is 148 with reactive CTG.

data_table.Vital signs: blood pressure 168/108, pulse 92, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Urine: protein/creatinine ratio 82 mg/mmol (<30), no blood, no leukocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give IV labetalol 20 mg bolus, load magnesium sulfate 4 g IV, admit for delivery within 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia at 34+ weeks with severe hypertension, symptoms and heavy proteinuria requires acute BP control (IV labetalol 20 to 40 mg or IV hydralazine), magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis, and planned delivery within 24 to 48 hours after corticosteroid completion is not required after 34+0. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Start oral labetalol 200 mg 12-hourly, admit for expectant management with twice weekly review
options.rationale: Severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia (>=160/110 mmHg) requires rapid IV or fast-acting oral treatment to lower BP within 15 to 30 minutes; oral labetalol 12-hourly is too slow. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Perform an immediate category-1 caesarean section without acute BP control given severe hypertension present
options.rationale: Immediate delivery without prior BP control risks maternal stroke; acute treatment of severe hypertension precedes and continues through delivery. Vaginal delivery is not contraindicated when maternal and fetal condition allow. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Discharge home with sublingual nifedipine 10 mg as required and midwife visit tomorrow morning for repeat BP
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine causes precipitous BP drop and is not used in pre-eclampsia; discharge is unsafe given severe features (BP, symptoms, proteinuria) requiring inpatient monitoring and delivery planning. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Give IV frusemide 40 mg for oedema and start oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily as monotherapy
options.rationale: Frusemide is not first line and reduces already contracted intravascular volume in pre-eclampsia. Methyldopa is safe in pregnancy but its onset is slow and unsuitable for severe hypertension requiring rapid control. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia (BP >=160/110, symptoms, heavy proteinuria) at or beyond 34 weeks requires acute BP control with IV labetalol or hydralazine, magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis (4 g IV load then 1 g/hour), and planned delivery within 24 to 48 hours. Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity are not indicated after 34+0 weeks. Vaginal delivery is preferred when maternal and fetal status allow. Continuous CTG and strict fluid balance limited to 80 mL/hour reduce pulmonary oedema risk.
key_points: Severe BP threshold: >=160/110 mmHg treated with IV labetalol 20 to 40 mg or IV hydralazine 5 to 10 mg
Magnesium sulfate loading 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour for eclampsia prophylaxis
Delivery within 24 to 48 hours at or beyond 34+0 weeks with severe features
Fluid restriction 80 mL/hour to avoid pulmonary oedema
explanation.pearls: Target BP after treatment is 140 to 150 / 80 to 100 mmHg to avoid placental hypoperfusion; overshoot toward normotension in a chronically hypertensive placenta can cause acute fetal distress.

stem: You are the GP obstetric shared-care doctor reviewing a 34-year-old G2P1 at her booking visit at 10+3 weeks. Her previous pregnancy was complicated by pre-eclampsia at 33 weeks requiring preterm delivery. She has chronic hypertension controlled on labetalol 200 mg twice daily and a BMI of 33. She has no bleeding disorder, no aspirin allergy, and no history of peptic ulcer disease. She is a non-smoker. Her BP today is 132/84 with urine dipstick clear.

data_table.Vital signs: blood pressure 132/84, pulse 78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, weight 88 kg
data_table.History: Previous PET at 33 weeks, chronic HTN on labetalol, BMI 33, no aspirin allergy, no peptic ulcer
data_table.Bloods: Hb 128 g/L (110-140), platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 62 umol/L (45-90), no proteinuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylactic recommendation?

options.text: Defer aspirin until 20+0 weeks when placental circulation matures and start at a dose of 75 mg once daily
options.rationale: Aspirin started after 16+0 weeks has substantially reduced benefit for PET prevention because trophoblast invasion is largely complete. Starting between 12+0 and 16+0 weeks gives maximal benefit. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Start aspirin 150 mg oral at night from 12+0 weeks and continue until 36+0 weeks gestation completed
options.rationale: SOMANZ and RANZCOG recommend low-dose aspirin (100 to 150 mg nocte, current evidence favours 150 mg) started between 12+0 and 16+0 weeks and continued until 36 to 37 weeks in women with one or more high-risk factors (prior PET, chronic HTN, CKD, autoimmune disease, diabetes) OR two or more moderate risk factors. This patient has two high-risk factors. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Prescribe elemental calcium 1.5 g daily as first-line prevention instead of aspirin due to safety profile
options.rationale: Calcium supplementation reduces PET risk primarily in women with low dietary calcium intake. In an Australian setting with adequate calcium intake, aspirin is the preferred prophylaxis in high-risk women. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Advise conservative dietary sodium restriction to below 2 g per day and no pharmacological prophylaxis required
options.rationale: Sodium restriction does not reduce PET risk and may worsen intravascular volume depletion. This patient has clear indications for aspirin prophylaxis given prior PET plus chronic HTN. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

options.text: Prescribe enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily throughout pregnancy for placental insufficiency prevention
options.rationale: LMWH is not indicated for PET prevention alone; its use in pregnancy is for VTE prophylaxis or antiphospholipid syndrome. Aspirin is the correct choice for PET prophylaxis in this patient. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Low-dose aspirin (100 to 150 mg nocte, 150 mg preferred) started between 12+0 and 16+0 weeks and continued until 36+0 weeks reduces the risk of pre-eclampsia by approximately 60 percent when started in early pregnancy in high-risk women. High-risk factors include prior PET, chronic hypertension, chronic kidney disease, pre-existing diabetes, and autoimmune disease. Two or more moderate risk factors (nulliparity, age >=40, BMI >=35, family history, IVF, multiple pregnancy interval) also indicate prophylaxis. The window is critical: starting after 16 weeks loses much of the benefit.
key_points: Start aspirin 100 to 150 mg at night between 12+0 and 16+0 weeks
Continue until 36+0 weeks (stop before delivery to reduce bleeding risk)
High-risk indication: prior PET, chronic HTN, CKD, diabetes, autoimmune disease
Calcium supplementation is second line in low-dietary-calcium populations
explanation.pearls: Aspirin 150 mg reduces preterm PET by approximately 62 percent (ASPRE trial 2017); the effect at term PET is smaller. Timing (before 16+0) matters more than dose within the 100 to 150 mg range.

stem: You are the ED registrar assessing a 26-year-old primigravida at 9+2 weeks with 5 days of persistent vomiting and inability to tolerate oral intake. She has lost 3.8 kg (5.2 percent of pre-pregnancy weight). She has no abdominal pain, no fever, no diarrhoea, no vaginal bleeding, and no dysuria. Urinalysis shows 3+ ketones and specific gravity 1.030 with no leukocytes or nitrites. Bedside ultrasound confirms a live intrauterine pregnancy consistent with dates with no adnexal mass. She has already tried oral ginger with no benefit.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 96/62, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Na 133 mmol/L (135-145), K 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), Cl 92 mmol/L (95-110), urea 8.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 68 umol/L (45-90), venous pH 7.48, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, urine ketones 3+

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Discharge on oral pyridoxine 40 mg TDS plus doxylamine 25 mg nocte with GP review the following morning
options.rationale: This patient has severe dehydration, hypokalaemia, ketonuria and metabolic alkalosis; discharge is unsafe. Admission for IV rehydration is warranted before oral therapy is likely to work. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

options.text: Give IV 5 percent dextrose 1 L over one hour then metoclopramide 10 mg IV before considering discharge from ED
options.rationale: Dextrose without preceding thiamine risks precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy in prolonged vomiting. Normal saline with potassium is preferred first, and thiamine must be given before any glucose load. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

options.text: Admit for IV normal saline with added potassium and give thiamine 100 mg IV before any dextrose containing fluid
options.rationale: Moderate to severe hyperemesis with dehydration and hypokalaemia requires IV rehydration with normal saline (avoid dextrose containing solutions initially) plus potassium replacement. Thiamine 100 mg IV must precede any dextrose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Add pyridoxine plus doxylamine and second-line antiemetic (ondansetron or metoclopramide) as pharmacotherapy. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for two weeks as first-line steroid therapy for refractory presentation today
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are considered only after failure of stepped pharmacotherapy including pyridoxine plus doxylamine, ondansetron and metoclopramide, and are avoided before 10 weeks due to a small oral cleft signal. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

options.text: Order urgent MRI brain to exclude posterior fossa lesion before any antiemetic therapy is commenced overnight
options.rationale: There are no neurological signs or atypical features to suggest raised intracranial pressure; investigations for secondary causes are reserved for unusual features. Empiric treatment for hyperemesis is appropriate here. (Source: RANZCOG Nausea Vomiting)

explanation.summary: Moderate to severe hyperemesis gravidarum (PUQE >=13, weight loss >5 percent, ketonuria, electrolyte disturbance) requires admission for IV rehydration with normal saline plus potassium and stepped antiemetic therapy: pyridoxine plus doxylamine, ondansetron (first trimester use is now considered safe in most guidance), metoclopramide. Thiamine 100 mg IV must precede any dextrose containing fluid to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory disease after 10 weeks.
key_points: IV normal saline with potassium; avoid initial dextrose without prior thiamine
Thiamine 100 mg IV before any glucose load in prolonged vomiting
Stepped antiemetics: pyridoxine + doxylamine, then ondansetron or metoclopramide
PUQE score categorises severity (mild <7, moderate 7 to 12, severe >=13)
explanation.pearls: Ondansetron in the first trimester carries a small absolute cardiac malformation signal (approximately 3 additional cases per 10,000 exposures) balanced against the harms of untreated severe hyperemesis; RANZCOG considers benefit outweighs risk with informed consent.

stem: You are the antenatal clinic registrar seeing a 30-year-old G3P2 at 30+1 weeks referred with tiredness and a haemoglobin of 92 g/L on routine bloods. She has previously tried oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily for the past 4 weeks but describes intolerable epigastric pain and constipation and admits to non-adherence for the last 2 weeks. She has no bleeding, no chronic disease, and no known haemoglobinopathy. Iron studies confirm iron deficiency. Her booking Hb was 116 g/L and she has no thalassaemia trait. She is not Rh negative.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Bloods: Hb 92 g/L (110-140), MCV 74 fL (80-100), ferritin 8 ug/L (30-200), transferrin saturation 8 percent (20-40)
data_table.History: Failed oral ferrous sulfate (intolerance), 30+1 weeks, no bleeding, no haemoglobinopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Increase oral ferrous sulfate to 325 mg three times daily and add ascorbic acid 500 mg to enhance absorption
options.rationale: Recent evidence favours alternate day dosing over multiple daily doses (hepcidin rise blocks absorption). She has documented intolerance; escalating is unlikely to succeed and IV iron is indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Refer for a two unit packed red blood cell transfusion this week to correct haemoglobin promptly for delivery
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic severe anaemia (Hb <70), haemodynamic compromise, or ongoing bleeding. Hb 92 with iron deficiency responds to IV iron with lower risk than transfusion. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Recommend dietary iron increase alone with red meat, leafy greens, and legumes daily and repeat FBE at 36 weeks
options.rationale: Dietary iron alone cannot correct established iron deficiency anaemia at 30 weeks with ferritin 8 in the required timeframe before delivery. Active replacement is required. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Arrange a single IV ferric carboxymaltose infusion of 1000 mg over 15 minutes as an outpatient day case
options.rationale: IV iron is indicated for iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy after 13 weeks when oral iron fails, is not tolerated, or when rapid replenishment is needed (>28 weeks with anaemia). Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg IV as a single dose is convenient and effective; ferric derisomaltose (Monofer) is an alternative. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

options.text: Start intramuscular iron sucrose 200 mg daily for 5 doses at the local community pharmacy over the coming week
options.rationale: Intramuscular iron is not routinely used in pregnancy (staining, pain, unreliable absorption). Iron sucrose IV requires multiple visits; ferric carboxymaltose or ferric derisomaltose allow single-dose replacement. (Source: RANZCOG Iron Deficiency)

explanation.summary: IV iron in pregnancy is indicated after the first trimester when oral iron fails, is not tolerated, or when replenishment before delivery is needed (typically >28 weeks with iron deficiency anaemia). Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg over 15 minutes and ferric derisomaltose 20 mg/kg allow single-dose replacement; iron sucrose requires multiple 200 mg doses. Anaphylaxis risk is very low with modern formulations but resuscitation facilities must be available. Oral iron alternate day dosing improves absorption over daily dosing (hepcidin biology).
key_points: IV iron indications: oral failure, intolerance, non-adherence, need for rapid correction >28 weeks
Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg over 15 minutes as single outpatient dose
Ferric derisomaltose 20 mg/kg alternative (higher single dose cap)
Transfusion reserved for Hb <70 or haemodynamic compromise
explanation.pearls: Hypophosphataemia after ferric carboxymaltose is common (approximately 40 percent) and may cause fatigue or bone pain; check phosphate 2 to 4 weeks post-infusion if symptomatic. Ferric derisomaltose has lower hypophosphataemia risk.

stem: You are the antenatal clinic doctor reviewing a 27-year-old primigravida at 14+2 weeks. Her routine midstream urine culture returned pure growth of Escherichia coli at 10^8 CFU/mL, sensitive to nitrofurantoin, cephalexin, trimethoprim, and amoxicillin. She has no urinary symptoms, no fever, no back pain, and no vaginal discharge. She has no drug allergies, no G6PD deficiency, no chronic kidney disease, and is not currently on any regular medications. She has never had a UTI before this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.MSU: E. coli 10^8 CFU/mL, sensitive nitrofurantoin, cephalexin, trimethoprim, amoxicillin
data_table.History: 14+2 weeks, no symptoms, no G6PD, no CKD, no allergies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic choice?

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 3 days with folic acid 5 mg daily due to interference with folate metabolism
options.rationale: Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester (folate antagonism, neural tube defect signal) and generally not used in pregnancy unless no alternative. At 14 weeks it is second choice. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

options.text: Fosfomycin 3 g single sachet orally taken on an empty stomach with 200 mL of water at bedtime for optimal effect
options.rationale: Fosfomycin single dose is an option in non-pregnant women but is not first line in Australian pregnancy guidance where 5 to 7 day treatment courses are recommended. Nitrofurantoin remains first line in the second trimester. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

options.text: Wait for symptoms to develop before treating and repeat MSU at 20 weeks to confirm bacteriuria persists longer
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy warrants treatment because up to 30 to 40 percent progress to pyelonephritis without therapy, and bacteriuria is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

options.text: Amoxicillin 500 mg orally 8-hourly for 5 days as first-line therapy because E. coli sensitivity is confirmed here
options.rationale: Amoxicillin resistance in community E. coli is around 50 percent even with reported susceptibility on some panels; nitrofurantoin or cephalexin are preferred first-line agents in pregnancy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

options.text: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6-hourly for 5 days and repeat MSU 1 to 2 weeks after treatment
options.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated to reduce pyelonephritis (60 percent risk if untreated) and preterm birth. Nitrofurantoin is first line in the second trimester (avoid at term and near delivery due to neonatal haemolysis risk). Duration is 5 to 7 days and a test of cure MSU is performed 1 to 2 weeks later. (Source: eTG Antibiotic UTI Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated because 20 to 40 percent progress to pyelonephritis and there is an association with preterm birth. Nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 5 days is first line in the second trimester; cephalexin 500 mg 6-hourly for 5 days is an alternative. Nitrofurantoin is avoided at term (34 weeks onward) and near delivery because of neonatal haemolysis risk. Trimethoprim is avoided in the first trimester due to folate antagonism. A test of cure MSU is performed 1 to 2 weeks after treatment.
key_points: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy to prevent pyelonephritis and preterm birth
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO 6-hourly for 5 days first line in second trimester
Avoid nitrofurantoin from 34 weeks onward (neonatal haemolysis)
Test of cure MSU 1 to 2 weeks after treatment
explanation.pearls: In G6PD deficiency, nitrofurantoin causes haemolysis at any gestation. In this cohort choose cephalexin 500 mg 6-hourly for 5 days or amoxicillin plus clavulanate 500/125 mg 8-hourly (based on susceptibility) instead.

stem: You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 25-year-old G1P0 following suction curettage yesterday for a confirmed complete hydatidiform mole diagnosed on ultrasound (snowstorm appearance) with a pre-operative beta hCG of 285,000 IU/L. Histology has confirmed complete mole. She is otherwise well, no bleeding, and observations are normal. She is not on any contraception and asks about future pregnancy plans. She reports her partner is very keen for a family soon.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 74, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: beta hCG 285000 IU/L pre-op, Hb 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Imaging: Preoperative USS: snowstorm appearance, no adnexal mass, no theca lutein cysts, empty uterus post-evacuation on today's scan

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow-up plan?

options.text: Serial serum beta hCG weekly until three negative results then monthly for 6 months, effective contraception advised
options.rationale: Complete mole surveillance is weekly serum beta hCG until three consecutive normal results then monthly for 6 months. Effective contraception (COCP or condoms; avoid IUD until hCG normal) prevents pregnancy that would confound hCG surveillance and delay recognition of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN). (Source: RANZCOG GTD)

options.text: Discharge with GP follow-up if any bleeding recurs; no formal hCG monitoring required after evacuation is complete
options.rationale: Surveillance is essential to detect GTN, which affects 15 to 20 percent of complete moles and 1 to 5 percent of partial moles. Missing follow-up delays chemotherapy for treatable disease. (Source: RANZCOG GTD)

options.text: Start prophylactic methotrexate 50 mg IM weekly for 8 weeks as chemoprophylaxis to reduce recurrence risk
options.rationale: Prophylactic chemotherapy is not routinely recommended; surveillance identifies those needing treatment and avoids unnecessary chemotherapy in most patients. (Source: RANZCOG GTD)

options.text: Insert copper intrauterine device today to provide long-acting reversible contraception during monitoring
options.rationale: IUD insertion is deferred until beta hCG has normalised, as insertion trauma and rare uterine perforation of residual disease raise concerns about persistence detection and haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG GTD)

options.text: Arrange staging CT thorax, abdomen and pelvis this week to exclude metastatic gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
options.rationale: Staging imaging is performed when GTN is diagnosed (plateau or rise in hCG, histological features) not routinely after evacuation of a mole with expected declining hCG. (Source: RANZCOG GTD)

explanation.summary: After suction evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole, serum beta hCG is monitored weekly until three consecutive normal results, then monthly for 6 months. Effective contraception (COCP or barrier) is used to prevent pregnancy that would confound surveillance; IUD is avoided until hCG is normal. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia develops in 15 to 20 percent of complete moles and requires methotrexate or actinomycin D. Referral to a specialist GTD service is recommended.
key_points: Weekly beta hCG until 3 normal results then monthly for 6 months (complete mole)
Partial mole: weekly until 3 normal then discharge
Effective contraception during surveillance; avoid IUD until hCG normal
15 to 20 percent of complete moles develop GTN needing chemotherapy
explanation.pearls: FIGO criteria for GTN after mole: hCG plateau over 4 measurements 3 weeks apart, hCG rise >=10 percent over 3 measurements 2 weeks apart, hCG persisting >=6 months after evacuation, or histological choriocarcinoma.

stem: You are the community psychiatry registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman with confirmed bipolar I disorder, currently euthymic 4 weeks after a hypomanic episode. She has had two clear manic episodes and one depressive episode in the past 3 years. The consultant recommends starting lithium for maintenance. She has no significant medical history, is not pregnant (LMP 1 week ago, using condoms consistently), is a non-smoker, and drinks 4 standard drinks weekly. She takes no regular medications and has no known allergies. She wants to complete her studies and eventually plan a pregnancy in 2 to 3 years.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.History: Bipolar I, 2 manic + 1 depressive episodes over 3 years, currently euthymic, LMP 1 week ago, no meds, no comorbidities

lead_in: Which baseline investigation set is most appropriate before starting lithium?

options.text: Full blood count, C-reactive protein, HbA1c, and vitamin B12 only; no imaging or ECG required before initiation
options.rationale: This omits renal function, TFTs, calcium, ECG and pregnancy test which are the specific relevant tests for lithium. Adding non-specific tests instead misses the target organs affected by lithium. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Urea, creatinine, electrolytes, thyroid function, calcium, ECG, pregnancy test, and weight recorded today
options.rationale: Standard pre-lithium workup includes renal function (baseline for later comparison), TFTs (lithium causes hypothyroidism in 20 percent), calcium (hyperparathyroidism association), ECG in patients with cardiac risk or age >40 (also for baseline QT), pregnancy test (lithium is teratogenic; Ebstein anomaly signal), and weight. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: MRI brain and EEG to rule out structural or epileptic conditions before beginning any mood stabiliser treatment
options.rationale: MRI and EEG are not routine pre-lithium workup; they are reserved for atypical clinical features or first-episode workup where organic disease is suspected. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: 24-hour urine collection for creatinine clearance and iothalamate GFR before every mood stabiliser starts today
options.rationale: 24-hour collection and iothalamate GFR are not routine baseline tests. Serum creatinine with eGFR is standard; more detailed renal testing is reserved for suspected chronic kidney disease. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Fasting lipids, iron studies, HbA1c, and echocardiogram are all required baseline tests before starting lithium
options.rationale: Lipids, iron and HbA1c are relevant for antipsychotic metabolic monitoring, not lithium. Echocardiogram is not routine unless cardiac disease is suspected. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

explanation.summary: Pre-lithium baseline workup targets the organs lithium affects: renal function (UEC and eGFR), thyroid function (hypothyroidism in 20 percent), calcium (hyperparathyroidism), ECG if age >40 or cardiac risk, pregnancy test (Ebstein anomaly and other teratogenicity), and weight. During treatment lithium levels are checked 5 to 7 days after each dose change and every 3 months once stable, with UEC/TFTs/calcium every 6 months. Trough level target is 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance; 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L for acute mania.
key_points: Baseline: UEC, TFTs, calcium, ECG (age >40 or cardiac risk), pregnancy test, weight
Ongoing: lithium level 12 hours post-dose, every 3 months once stable
UEC, TFTs, calcium every 6 months during maintenance
Maintenance target 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L; acute mania 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L
explanation.pearls: Lithium clearance falls approximately 15 percent for every 10-year age increase after 40 and rises 30 to 50 percent in pregnancy (dose usually increased in T2/T3, halved immediately before delivery); check level within 12 hours of birth.

stem: You are the ED registrar assessing a 19-year-old university student brought in by parents with a 3 week history of paranoid delusions (belief he is being tracked), auditory hallucinations, and social withdrawal. He denies substance use but parents suspect cannabis. He has no fever, no headache, no neurological symptoms, no seizures, and no recent travel. He is on no medications and has no personal or family history of psychiatric illness. He appears clinically well hydrated and oriented. Physical and neurological examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.MSE: Thought-disordered, paranoid delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations, blunted affect, cognition intact
data_table.Neuro: GCS 15, cranial nerves intact, no focal deficits, no meningism, no movement abnormalities

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation set?

options.text: MRI brain with contrast and lumbar puncture for CSF anti-NMDA antibodies on every first episode of psychosis case
options.rationale: MRI and LP are indicated when features suggest anti-NMDA encephalitis (movement disorder, seizures, autonomic instability, rapid cognitive decline) or other structural or inflammatory disease, not routinely on all FEP. (Source: RANZCP Psychosis)

options.text: 24-hour urinary catecholamines and metanephrines to rule out phaeochromocytoma-related psychiatric manifestations
options.rationale: Phaeochromocytoma presents with paroxysmal hypertension, headaches, palpitations and sweating rather than psychotic symptoms. This is not routine FEP workup. (Source: RANZCP Psychosis)

options.text: FBC, UEC, LFTs, CRP, TFTs, B12/folate, urine drug screen, hCG if appropriate, and CT brain if focal signs
options.rationale: First-episode psychosis workup screens for organic causes: metabolic (UEC, calcium, LFTs, TSH, B12/folate), infection (FBC, CRP), substances (UDS), and structural pathology (CT/MRI only if focal signs, atypical features, or age extremes). Routine MRI/EEG on all FEP is not evidence based but is common practice; national guidance requires imaging when clinically indicated. (Source: RANZCP Psychosis)

options.text: PET scan of the brain to characterise dopamine receptor availability before commencing any antipsychotic therapy
options.rationale: Dopamine PET is a research tool; it does not guide antipsychotic choice or diagnosis in routine clinical care. (Source: RANZCP Psychosis)

options.text: Full lupus autoantibody panel including ANA, dsDNA, ENA, complement, ANCA at the first ED assessment routinely
options.rationale: Autoimmune workup is targeted to clinical features suggesting cerebral lupus or vasculitis (skin, joints, rash, renal signs), not routine for all FEP presentations. (Source: RANZCP Psychosis)

explanation.summary: First-episode psychosis workup screens targeted organic causes: metabolic (UEC, calcium, LFTs, TSH, B12/folate), infection (FBC, CRP), substances (urine drug screen), and structural (CT/MRI when focal signs, atypical features, or first psychosis in older adults). Neuroimaging is not universally required in young patients with a typical presentation, but is commonly done. Anti-NMDA encephalitis is considered when there is a movement disorder, seizure, autonomic dysfunction, or rapid cognitive decline. Early referral to an early psychosis service and offer of low-dose second-generation antipsychotic are core actions.
key_points: Screen: UEC, LFTs, calcium, TFTs, B12/folate, FBC, CRP, urine drug screen, glucose
Neuroimaging: focal signs, atypical features, first psychosis after age 40
Consider anti-NMDA encephalitis if movement, autonomic, seizure features
Refer to early psychosis intervention service
explanation.pearls: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis triggers include ovarian teratoma (young women 60 percent) and herpes simplex virus infection; screening pelvic ultrasound is indicated when this is suspected.

stem: You are the psychiatric registrar admitting a 28-year-old man with 6 days of florid mania: elevated mood, grandiose delusions of being a business magnate, 2 hours sleep per night, pressured speech, and disinhibited spending. He has a 2 year history of bipolar I with 3 prior admissions. He is not on any current mood stabiliser (stopped lithium 6 months ago due to weight gain). He has no medical comorbidities, no substance use, and is not planning fatherhood. He is willing to take oral medication.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 98, blood pressure 132/82, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.MSE: Elevated mood, grandiose delusions, pressured speech, flight of ideas, no active psychotic threat
data_table.Bloods: UEC, LFTs, TSH, calcium all normal; beta hCG not applicable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily titrated to therapeutic dose plus zolpidem 10 mg nocte for sleep for two weeks
options.rationale: SSRIs are contraindicated as monotherapy in acute mania because they can worsen or prolong mania. Antidepressants in bipolar are used only for depression with concurrent mood stabiliser cover. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Carbamazepine 200 mg oral BD titrated with therapeutic drug monitoring plus prazosin 1 mg for sleep at night
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is a second-line agent for mania and requires slow titration; it is not first-line. Prazosin is not indicated. Faster-acting agents are preferred in severe mania. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg TDS as monotherapy for 2 weeks until behavioural containment allows further treatment consideration
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine monotherapy does not treat mania; it manages agitation. A mood stabiliser or antipsychotic is essential to achieve remission. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg oral daily, titrating up over 3 days, with lorazepam 1 to 2 mg TDS for acute agitation and sleep
options.rationale: For acute mania, first-line monotherapy options include lithium, sodium valproate, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, and aripiprazole. Second-generation antipsychotics have faster onset than lithium (days vs 1 to 2 weeks) and are preferred in severe presentations. Adjunct benzodiazepine is standard for acute agitation and sleep. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Electroconvulsive therapy this week as first-line treatment before any trial of pharmacological options is undertaken
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective for mania but is reserved for treatment-resistant cases, severe features (life-threatening exhaustion, catatonia, refusal of intake), or when rapid response is essential and pharmacotherapy has failed or is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for acute mania includes lithium, sodium valproate, or a second-generation antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, aripiprazole, asenapine). Second-generation antipsychotics act faster than lithium (days vs 1 to 2 weeks) and are preferred in severe presentations. Adjunct benzodiazepine (lorazepam 1 to 2 mg TDS PRN) manages agitation and sleep. SSRIs are contraindicated in acute mania. ECT is reserved for severe or refractory cases. Discuss teratogenicity of sodium valproate with reproductive-age patients.
key_points: First-line: lithium, valproate, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, aripiprazole
Second-generation antipsychotics preferred for rapid onset in severe mania
Adjunct lorazepam 1 to 2 mg TDS for agitation and sleep
SSRIs contraindicated; ECT reserved for refractory or severe cases
explanation.pearls: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless a Pregnancy Prevention Programme is in place and no alternative exists (TGA and PBS restrictions from 2023 apply).

stem: You are the GP seeing a 34-year-old man 4 months after a serious motor vehicle accident. He describes intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance of driving, hypervigilance and irritability. Symptoms are causing occupational impairment. He has no current mood disorder criteria met, no active substance misuse, and no suicidal ideation. He has no significant past psychiatric history and no current medications. He asks how to get better without medication if possible.

data_table.History: MVA 4 months ago, meets DSM-5-TR PTSD criteria, occupational impairment, no comorbid MDD or SUD
data_table.MSE: Anxious mood, congruent affect, no psychotic features, cognition intact, no self-harm
data_table.Function: Off work 3 months, avoiding driving, sleep 4 hours per night

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment recommendation?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily titrated to 100 mg after 2 weeks and continued for at least 12 months as monotherapy
options.rationale: SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) are effective but are second choice to trauma-focused psychotherapy in Australian guidance. They are appropriate when psychotherapy is declined or unavailable, or as adjunct. (Source: Phoenix PTSD)

options.text: Prazosin 1 mg orally nocte, titrated for nightmares, as sole intervention without psychotherapy or SSRI cover
options.rationale: Prazosin is an adjunct for PTSD-related nightmares, not a first-line PTSD treatment. It should be added to trauma-focused psychotherapy or SSRI, not used alone. (Source: Phoenix PTSD)

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg TDS for 6 weeks to reduce hyperarousal symptoms and improve sleep architecture during recovery period
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not recommended for PTSD; they do not treat core symptoms, worsen dissociation, impair therapy engagement, and cause dependence. (Source: Phoenix PTSD)

options.text: Quetiapine 50 mg nocte for insomnia and low-dose paroxetine for daytime symptoms with weekly follow up review
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first-line for PTSD; combination pharmacotherapy from the outset is not recommended. Psychotherapy is preferred first with pharmacotherapy considered second line. (Source: Phoenix PTSD)

options.text: Trauma-focused CBT (or EMDR) with weekly sessions over 8 to 12 weeks as first-line evidence-based psychotherapy
options.rationale: The Australian PTSD guidelines (Phoenix Australia) recommend trauma-focused CBT (including prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy) or EMDR as first-line treatment, delivered weekly for approximately 8 to 12 sessions. Pharmacotherapy (SSRI/SNRI) is offered when psychotherapy is declined, unavailable, or insufficient. (Source: Phoenix PTSD)

explanation.summary: Trauma-focused psychological therapies (trauma-focused CBT including prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy, and EMDR) are first-line evidence-based treatments for adult PTSD, typically weekly for 8 to 12 sessions. SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) and the SNRI venlafaxine are effective and used when psychotherapy is declined or unavailable, or as adjunct. Benzodiazepines are not recommended (no efficacy, dependence risk, dissociation). Prazosin can be added for treatment-resistant nightmares.
key_points: First-line: trauma-focused CBT (PE, CPT) or EMDR, 8 to 12 weekly sessions
Pharmacotherapy: SSRI (sertraline, paroxetine) or SNRI (venlafaxine) if psychotherapy declined or insufficient
Avoid benzodiazepines in PTSD
Prazosin adjunct for refractory nightmares only
explanation.pearls: In veterans and refugees with complex PTSD, phased treatment (safety and stabilisation before trauma processing) is emphasised by Phoenix Australia; jumping straight to exposure without stabilisation increases risk of dropout.

stem: You are the GP seeing a 48-year-old woman on alprazolam 1 mg three times daily for 6 years, initially started for panic disorder. She wants to reduce and eventually stop. She has no current alcohol misuse, no seizure history, and no current mood disorder criteria met. She has partner support and is committed to a slow taper. She has no active plans to conceive and has no other benzodiazepines or z-drugs prescribed. She is otherwise well and on no other regular medications.

data_table.History: Alprazolam 1 mg TDS for 6 years, wants to stop, no alcohol misuse, no seizures, no MDD, supportive partner
data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76, blood pressure 122/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.MSE: Anxious but not depressed, no psychosis, no active self-harm, cognition intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management strategy?

options.text: Convert to equivalent diazepam and reduce by 10 percent of the current dose every 2 to 4 weeks with monitoring
options.rationale: The RACGP recommends conversion to equivalent long-acting diazepam (alprazolam 1 mg = diazepam 20 mg approximately, so 3 mg alprazolam ~ 60 mg diazepam) then gradual reduction of 10 percent per 2 to 4 weeks with adjustment based on symptoms. Slower reduction (1 to 2 mg per fortnight) may be needed near the end. Total taper often takes 6 to 12 months. (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence)

options.text: Stop alprazolam abruptly today and prescribe zopiclone 7.5 mg nocte for sleep for 4 weeks then review the taper
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of a high-potency short-acting benzodiazepine after long use risks severe withdrawal including seizures and delirium. Substitution with a z-drug does not prevent withdrawal. (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence)

options.text: Add mirtazapine 30 mg nocte and continue current alprazolam dose indefinitely because it is providing symptomatic relief
options.rationale: Long-term benzodiazepine use for anxiety carries risks (falls, cognitive impairment, dependence, mortality) and is not indicated as chronic treatment. The patient has decided to stop, which is the correct decision. (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence)

options.text: Refer for inpatient detoxification and admission for rapid clonidine-assisted withdrawal over a 7 to 10 day period
options.rationale: Rapid withdrawal is generally not recommended for benzodiazepine dependence; gradual outpatient taper is preferred and safer. Inpatient care is reserved for complex cases or failed outpatient tapers. (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence)

options.text: Prescribe flumazenil infusion in a monitored day-stay unit to accelerate receptor recovery over a 4 to 7 day admission
options.rationale: Flumazenil infusion protocols are not standard care in Australia; risks include seizure and rebound withdrawal. Gradual taper on equivalent diazepam remains the evidence-based approach. (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence)

explanation.summary: Long-term benzodiazepine dependence is managed by conversion to an equivalent dose of long-acting diazepam and gradual reduction of 10 percent per 2 to 4 weeks with symptom-guided pace, often taking 6 to 12 months. Slower steps near the end (0.5 to 1 mg reductions) improve success. Substitute psychological treatment (CBT for panic) and address sleep hygiene. Abrupt cessation risks seizures, delirium, and rebound anxiety. Alprazolam and other high-potency short-acting agents are especially difficult; conversion to diazepam smooths withdrawal.
key_points: Convert to equivalent diazepam (alprazolam 1 mg ~ diazepam 20 mg)
Reduce by 10 percent every 2 to 4 weeks, symptom-guided pace
Total taper typically 6 to 12 months; slower steps near end
Avoid abrupt cessation (seizure, delirium, rebound anxiety)
explanation.pearls: Panic disorder responds to SSRI (sertraline) or SNRI plus CBT; establishing this before or during taper reduces relapse. Alprazolam is on the S8 (controlled) list in Australia; consider TGA and state authority requirements when prescribing long-term.

stem: You are the GP seeing a 68-year-old woman with new persistent atrial fibrillation confirmed on 12-lead ECG and Holter. She has hypertension (on perindopril), type 2 diabetes (on metformin, HbA1c 7.0 percent), and no history of stroke, heart failure, vascular disease, or bleeding. Her BP today is 132/82, weight 78 kg, and creatinine 82 umol/L (eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2). She has no significant valvular heart disease on echo. She is symptomatic with palpitations but rate is controlled at 88 bpm on bisoprolol.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88 irregular, blood pressure 132/82, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.History: New persistent AF, HTN, T2DM, no stroke/HF/vascular disease, no bleeding history
data_table.Bloods: creatinine 82 umol/L (45-90), eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m^2, HbA1c 7.0 percent, weight 78 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate stroke prevention strategy?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily as antithrombotic therapy for atrial fibrillation with the score less than four total
options.rationale: Aspirin does not provide adequate stroke prevention in AF and is no longer recommended. It carries bleeding risk without stroke reduction benefit. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)

options.text: Start apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily long-term unless a specific contraindication develops during ongoing review
options.rationale: CHA2DS2-VA score is 3 (age 65 to 74 = 1, HTN = 1, DM = 1) indicating clear anticoagulation benefit. NOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, rivaroxaban) is first choice over warfarin in non-valvular AF. Apixaban 5 mg BD is standard unless dose reduction criteria (age >=80, weight <=60 kg, creatinine >=133 umol/L, with at least 2 of 3) are met. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)

options.text: No antithrombotic therapy since the annual stroke risk is low enough to permit conservative management strategy
options.rationale: CHA2DS2-VA of 3 confers an annual stroke risk of approximately 3.2 percent; anticoagulation reduces this substantially and is clearly indicated. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)

options.text: Warfarin targeting INR 2.5 with weekly monitoring by community pathology and pharmacist-led dose adjustment
options.rationale: Warfarin is second choice in non-valvular AF; NOACs are preferred for equivalent or superior efficacy, lower intracranial haemorrhage risk, and no INR monitoring. Warfarin remains first choice in mechanical valves and moderate to severe mitral stenosis. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)

options.text: Dual antiplatelet clopidogrel plus aspirin as an alternative to anticoagulation in patients with adequate rate control
options.rationale: Dual antiplatelet therapy is inferior to anticoagulation for stroke prevention in AF and carries substantial bleeding risk. It is not a substitute for anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA CSANZ AF)

explanation.summary: Non-valvular AF stroke prevention is guided by CHA2DS2-VA (Australia dropped the sex category in the 2018 NHFA/CSANZ update, now called CHA2DS2-VA). Score >=2 indicates NOAC therapy: apixaban 5 mg BD (2.5 BD if 2 of age >=80, weight <=60 kg, creatinine >=133), dabigatran 150 mg BD (110 BD if age >=75 or renal impairment), rivaroxaban 20 mg daily (15 mg if CrCl 30 to 49). Warfarin remains first line in mechanical valves and moderate to severe mitral stenosis. Aspirin and dual antiplatelet are not effective substitutes.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA >=2: NOAC first line in non-valvular AF
Apixaban 5 mg BD; reduce to 2.5 BD if 2 of (age >=80, weight <=60 kg, creatinine >=133)
Warfarin only for mechanical valves or moderate to severe mitral stenosis
Aspirin not recommended for AF stroke prevention
explanation.pearls: For elective procedures on apixaban, hold 24 hours before low bleeding-risk procedures and 48 hours before high bleeding-risk procedures with normal renal function; no bridging with LMWH is required.

stem: You are the ED registrar seeing a 68-year-old man brought in 2 hours after sudden right-sided weakness and dysphasia witnessed by his wife. NIHSS is 12 (right hemiparesis, expressive aphasia, gaze preference). He has hypertension (on ramipril) and is on aspirin 100 mg daily. He has no recent surgery, no head injury, no bleeding, no anticoagulation, and no seizure with onset. His INR is 1.0. BP is currently 168/94. CT brain shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct; CTA shows a proximal M1 occlusion on the left MCA.

data_table.Vital signs: blood pressure 168/94, pulse 82 regular, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Investigations: CT brain no haemorrhage or established infarct; CTA left M1 occlusion; BSL 6.8 mmol/L; INR 1.0; platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give aspirin 300 mg orally now, admit to stroke unit, arrange elective thrombectomy tomorrow morning after MRI
options.rationale: Delaying thrombectomy in a patient with proximal LVO within the treatment window costs salvageable brain. Aspirin is not a substitute for thrombolysis or thrombectomy when both are indicated. (Source: Stroke Foundation)

options.text: Give IV labetalol 20 mg to lower blood pressure to below 140/80 before considering any reperfusion therapy option
options.rationale: Target BP before alteplase is <185/110, not <140/80. Aggressive BP lowering can worsen infarct extension by reducing collateral flow. (Source: Stroke Foundation)

options.text: Give IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (10 percent bolus, remainder over 60 min) plus arrange endovascular thrombectomy now
options.rationale: Within 4.5 hours of witnessed onset and no contraindications, IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg, 10 percent as bolus over 1 minute, remainder over 60 minutes) is standard. Proximal M1 occlusion with NIHSS 12 and imaging showing salvageable brain warrants concurrent endovascular thrombectomy (up to 6 hours from onset routinely; up to 24 hours with perfusion imaging showing mismatch). BP is treated to <185/110 before alteplase. (Source: Stroke Foundation)

options.text: Give IV heparin infusion to prevent clot propagation and reassess in 24 hours for further reperfusion candidacy
options.rationale: Early therapeutic anticoagulation is not beneficial and increases haemorrhage risk. Alteplase and thrombectomy are the reperfusion strategies. (Source: Stroke Foundation)

options.text: Withhold thrombolysis due to prior aspirin use and instead administer IV nimodipine and admit for expectant care
options.rationale: Aspirin use is not a contraindication to alteplase. Nimodipine is for subarachnoid haemorrhage vasospasm, not ischaemic stroke. (Source: Stroke Foundation)

explanation.summary: Acute ischaemic stroke reperfusion combines IV alteplase (within 4.5 hours; tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg is now guideline-endorsed as equivalent or superior in Australia) with endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation large vessel occlusion (within 6 hours routinely, up to 24 hours with favourable perfusion imaging). BP is treated to <185/110 before alteplase. Contraindications include haemorrhage, recent major surgery, prior intracerebral haemorrhage, active bleeding, INR >1.7 or NOAC use within window, platelets <100.
key_points: IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg within 4.5 hours (tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg equivalent in Australia)
Endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation LVO up to 6 hours (24 hours with imaging)
BP target <185/110 before thrombolysis; <180/105 during and 24 hours after
Aspirin use is NOT a contraindication to alteplase
explanation.pearls: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg as single IV bolus has replaced alteplase in many Australian stroke units; it is faster to administer (single bolus vs 60 minute infusion), does not delay transfer for thrombectomy, and shows equivalent or better outcomes in AcT and EXTEND-IA TNK trials.

stem: You are the ED registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman with a known history of asthma presenting with 6 hours of worsening breathlessness. She can speak in short phrases only. She has been using her salbutamol MDI hourly with minimal improvement. She has no fever, no chest pain, no haemoptysis, and no recent COVID or influenza-like illness. She has never been intubated for asthma. She takes budesonide/formoterol 200/6 mcg twice daily but admits variable adherence. She has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, respiratory rate 30, blood pressure 122/76, SpO2 90% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Widespread wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase, accessory muscle use, no cyanosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Non-invasive ventilation with BiPAP settings 12/6 as first-line management before any bronchodilator escalation attempted
options.rationale: NIV in acute asthma has limited evidence and can worsen air trapping and hyperinflation. Bronchodilator therapy, oxygen, and steroids are first line. Intubation is considered for exhaustion or CO2 rise. (Source: NAC AAMH)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days plus a salbutamol MDI with spacer 4 puffs 4-hourly and outpatient GP follow-up
options.rationale: Antibiotics are not routinely indicated unless there is evidence of bacterial infection. Discharge is unsafe in acute severe asthma; the patient requires immediate escalated bronchodilator therapy and steroids. (Source: NAC AAMH)

options.text: IV theophylline 250 mg loading dose over 20 min as first-line bronchodilator before nebulised salbutamol trial
options.rationale: Theophylline is not first line and has a narrow therapeutic index. Nebulised salbutamol plus ipratropium, oxygen, and systemic corticosteroid are the first-line management. (Source: NAC AAMH)

options.text: Salbutamol 5 mg plus ipratropium 500 mcg nebulised, oxygen to target 93 to 95 percent, and oral prednisolone 50 mg
options.rationale: Acute severe asthma (unable to complete sentences, RR >=25, HR >=110, SpO2 <92 percent, PEF 33 to 50 percent) is treated with continuous or back-to-back nebulised salbutamol plus ipratropium, controlled oxygen to target SpO2 93 to 95 percent, oral prednisolone 50 mg (or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg if oral not tolerated), and IV magnesium sulfate 2 g if no rapid improvement. (Source: NAC AAMH)

options.text: Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM to lateral thigh as initial bronchodilator therapy before nebulised beta-agonist administration
options.rationale: IM adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis or life-threatening asthma with imminent arrest. It is not first line in acute severe asthma when nebulised salbutamol can be delivered. (Source: NAC AAMH)

explanation.summary: Acute severe asthma is treated with continuous or back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg (or MDI plus spacer 4 to 12 puffs) with ipratropium 500 mcg added for severe exacerbations, controlled oxygen to target SpO2 93 to 95 percent (avoid hyperoxia), and systemic corticosteroid (prednisolone 50 mg oral or hydrocortisone 100 mg IV) within 1 hour. IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes is added if no rapid improvement. Life-threatening features (silent chest, cyanosis, bradycardia, exhaustion, altered LOC, PEF <33 percent) prompt ICU escalation and consideration of intubation.
key_points: Salbutamol 5 mg + ipratropium 500 mcg nebulised, controlled O2 to SpO2 93 to 95 percent
Prednisolone 50 mg oral (or hydrocortisone 100 mg IV) within 1 hour
IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min if no rapid improvement
ICU review for life-threatening features (silent chest, exhaustion, altered LOC, PEF <33 percent)
explanation.pearls: Discharge criteria after acute asthma: PEF >=75 percent predicted or personal best, stable on 4-hourly bronchodilator, review of technique and adherence, prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 to 7 days total, written action plan, and follow-up within 2 to 7 days.

stem: You are the GP seeing a 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 8 years, on metformin 1 g twice daily, with an HbA1c of 8.4 percent (target <7 percent). He has hypertension (on perindopril), stable ischaemic heart disease with prior MI 3 years ago (on aspirin, atorvastatin, bisoprolol), and eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m^2. His weight is 94 kg (BMI 31), BP 128/78, and there is no diabetic ketoacidosis, no recurrent UTI or genital infection, and no history of DKA-precipitating illness. He has good renal function and no diabetic foot ulcers.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, weight 94 kg
data_table.Bloods: HbA1c 8.4 percent, eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m^2, creatinine 92 umol/L (60-110), LDL 1.8 mmol/L on statin
data_table.Comorbidity: Prior MI 3 years ago, HTN, no DKA history, no recurrent GU infections, no foot ulcers

lead_in: What is the most appropriate add-on to metformin?

options.text: Add gliclazide MR 60 mg oral daily titrated up over 6 weeks and continue metformin for glycaemic control only
options.rationale: Sulfonylureas do not provide cardiovascular benefit and carry hypoglycaemia and weight gain risks. In a patient with established ASCVD, SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA is preferred as second line. (Source: RACGP Diabetes)

options.text: Add basal insulin glargine 10 units subcutaneously nocte titrated by 2 units every 3 days for glycaemic control
options.rationale: Insulin is added when other options have failed or in specific circumstances (severe hyperglycaemia, symptomatic). It causes hypoglycaemia and weight gain without cardiovascular benefit. Cardioprotective agent first. (Source: RACGP Diabetes)

options.text: Add pioglitazone 30 mg oral daily to improve insulin sensitivity and continue metformin for durable glycaemic control
options.rationale: Pioglitazone carries risks of heart failure, weight gain, fractures, and bladder cancer signal. It is not preferred over SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA in patients with ASCVD. (Source: RACGP Diabetes)

options.text: Add sitagliptin 100 mg oral daily as weight-neutral therapy with low hypoglycaemia risk and continue metformin fully
options.rationale: DPP-4 inhibitors are weight neutral with low hypoglycaemia but do not provide cardiovascular protection. In ASCVD, SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA is preferred as second line. (Source: RACGP Diabetes)

options.text: Add empagliflozin 10 mg oral daily and continue metformin for combined cardiovascular and glycaemic benefit
options.rationale: In T2DM with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, an SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) or GLP-1 receptor agonist (semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide) with proven cardiovascular benefit is added regardless of HbA1c. Empagliflozin reduces cardiovascular death, MI, stroke, and heart failure hospitalisation (EMPA-REG). (Source: RACGP Diabetes)

explanation.summary: In type 2 diabetes with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease, an SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) or GLP-1 receptor agonist (semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide) with proven cardiovascular or renal benefit is added regardless of HbA1c. SGLT2 inhibitors are preferred in heart failure and CKD; GLP-1 RA give greater HbA1c and weight reduction. Both reduce major adverse cardiovascular events. Sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, and insulin remain useful for glycaemic control without cardioprotective benefit.
key_points: T2DM + ASCVD: add SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA regardless of HbA1c
SGLT2i preferred in heart failure and CKD (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin)
GLP-1 RA give greater HbA1c and weight reduction (semaglutide, dulaglutide)
Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain, no CV benefit
explanation.pearls: SGLT2 inhibitor sick day rules: withhold during acute illness, dehydration, fasting, and surgery to reduce euglycaemic DKA risk. Warn about mycotic genital infections (approximately 5 to 10 percent, more in women) and rare Fournier's gangrene.
